extracted.intended_audience: public health press officers, health researchers, and journalists
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for preparing and assessing press releases about health research (especially rapid reviews and COVID-19 reports), and for journalists reporting on them. Focuses on accuracy, framing, inclusion of evidence and expert quotes, and engagement between public bodies and media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include all important evidence in the PR
rubrics_metrics.description: All important evidence should be available in the PR, reducing any additional steps or barriers to access the information or interpret scientific outputs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors state it was extremely rare that media reporting would include information that was in the research report and not in the PR; therefore PRs should contain the key evidence to avoid secondary-source loss. Make primary findings and key study details directly available in the PR so journalists do not need additional steps to access or interpret outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide brief supplemental public health and epidemiological education
rubrics_metrics.description: Include brief supplemental public health and epidemiological education within PRs to help journalists and the public interpret technical findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is recommended because coverage of PR4 demonstrated misunderstandings of epidemiological data collection, monitoring, and analysis. Supplemental explanations of methods, limitations, and interpretation can reduce misinterpretation, particularly for rapid reviews and technical results that journalists may be less familiar with.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure rigour and accuracy in PR wording
rubrics_metrics.description: PRs announcing health research results should be rigorous and accurate in their presentation of findings and limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper emphasises the need for rigour and accuracy in health-research related PRs, noting that redundant reporting across outlets is acceptable only if the original PR is of high quality. High-quality PRs promote consistent, accurate reporting across media sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage proactively with journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: Public bodies should better engage with journalists to support accurate and evidence-focused coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors argue for improved engagement because journalists act as intermediaries and can reframe messages; proactive engagement can help mitigate selective framing and ensure complex or caveated evidence is understood and communicated appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid selective reporting and selective quoting that change messages
rubrics_metrics.description: PRs and journalists should guard against selective coverage and selective quoting of stakeholders that alter the intended evidence-focused message into an emotion- or opinion-driven narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study found selective reporting and interplay of stakeholder quotes frequently changed narratives (e.g., political enthusiasm vs. public health caution). Ensure PRs present balanced key messages and make relevant caveats and context prominent so selective quoting is less likely to mislead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include appropriate caveats and limitations (do not fear reduced coverage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly present caveats and limitations within PRs; including caveats does not necessarily reduce newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors did not find a clear pattern that caveating reduced news coverage — heavily caveated reports still received substantial attention. Therefore, PRs should transparently state study quality, limits, and uncertainty without concern that this will prevent media uptake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overstating causality or making inappropriate causal claims
rubrics_metrics.description: PRs and journalists should not make inappropriate causal interpretations of observational or review findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While the study observed that media largely did not make inappropriate causal interpretations (perhaps because many reports were reviews), the guideline remains that PRs should avoid language implying causation when the evidence does not support it, and journalists should not extrapolate beyond key messages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritise evidence-focused expert quotes over political or purely emotive quotes
rubrics_metrics.description: When choosing quotes to include, favour expert public health or researcher quotes that elucidate evidence rather than political or emotive quotes that may reframe findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper shows that frequent quoting of politicians or non-expert sources correlated with more emotion-based reporting and potential weakening of scientific authority. Including external expert quotes (not just PR-supplied quotes) may improve accuracy and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious with human-interest framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid over-reliance on human-interest or emotional framing that can give disproportionate attention to single stories and mislead about the general state of evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Human-interest frames (emotional appeals, gain framing) increase the likelihood a PR is selected for coverage, but can mislead readers into overstating severity or importance. Use human elements judiciously and balance them with technical context and broader evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow established minimum requirements for clinical trial PRs
rubrics_metrics.description: Adhere to suggested minimum requirements for PRs announcing clinical trial results (especially COVID-19 trials).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors reference prior work proposing a list of minimum requirements for PRs about clinical trial results; PRs should follow such checklists (e.g., clear description of endpoints, limitations, peer-review status) and consider developing similar guidance for rapid reviews and other health research outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure accessibility of primary report content to journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the primary research report and any supplemental materials easily accessible so journalists can verify and go beyond the PR when necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study noted that media very rarely reported information present in the research report but absent from the PR. Providing direct links, summaries, and accessible supplementary data reduces barriers and supports accurate, in-depth reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept redundancy when PR quality is high; aim for consistent messaging
rubrics_metrics.description: Redundant verbatim or moderately edited copies of PR wording across outlets are acceptable if the PR is high quality, as this produces consistent reporting of study findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From an organisational communication perspective redundant reporting is not a concern so long as the PR is of high quality. Therefore, invest in clear, precise PR language that can be reliably reused by media.
